title: Robot versus zero-turn: the real coverage maths
customBody:
**Does a robot mower cover more ground than a zero-turn?**

Not per hour. A wide-deck zero-turn with an operator on it puts down more ground in an hour than a 48-inch tracked RTK mower does, and we'd rather say that plainly than dress it up.

**Per hour is the wrong unit**

A zero-turn's coverage depends on deck width and operator. Wider deck and faster ground speed means more acres an hour, and on open ground a good operator will keep that up all day.

The machine does about 8 acres (3 hectares) a day. That's our planning figure and we don't move it.

Here's the part that gets skipped in the comparison. The zero-turn covers ground while someone is sitting on it. The machine covers ground while nobody is.

**Hours and consistency**

RTK and LiDAR don't need daylight. The machine can run through the evening, through the night, and be partway through the next block before anyone turns up in the morning. We've written elsewhere about [why the best time to mow a solar farm is 2am](blog-the-best-time-to-mow-a-solar-farm-is-2am.html).

A zero-turn runs for the hours a person is on it. That's a real limit and a fair one. People have to go home.

**What the person does instead**

The machine doesn't do all of it. Close-in work around posts, structures and edges is 60 to 70 percent autonomous at best, and people finish the rest. Someone still sets the machine up, moves it between blocks, keeps the blades right and sorts it out when it stops.

That's a skilled local technician role. The difference is where the hours land: less time driving in straight lines, more time on the work that needs judgement.

The machine cuts the same line at 6am and at 6pm. It doesn't get tired at the end of a long block, doesn't cut wide on the last pass and doesn't rush a Friday afternoon. That matters more across a repeating cycle than it does on a single visit.

**Where the robot loses**

Dense summer grass over 300 mm roughly halves speed. Both machine types. The machine gets no exemption.

Small blocks where transport and setup eat the day. Tight, cluttered ground with a lot of edge relative to open area. Jobs that need finishing today, once, and never again. On those a zero-turn with a good operator is the right tool, and we'd tell you so.

Our model is to operate machines where there's enough planned, repeating work to be worth the setup. Not everywhere.

**Common questions**

### How many acres a day can an autonomous mower do?

We plan on about 8 acres (3 hectares) a day per machine. Dense summer grass over 300 mm roughly halves that.

### Can it really run at night?

Yes. RTK positioning and LiDAR don't need daylight. The machine keeps working after the crew has gone home.

### Does it replace the ride-on?

No. It takes the open repeatable passes. A zero-turn still earns its place on small, cluttered or one-off jobs.

### What about edges and posts?

People do those. Close-in work runs 60 to 70 percent autonomous and the rest is finished by hand.

**Read next**

Related: [Eight acres a day. Not twelve.](blog-eight-acres-a-day-not-twelve.html), [A week a month on the slasher](blog-a-week-a-month-on-the-slasher.html) and [Autonomous Mowing vs Traditional Ride-On: A Property Owner's Guide](blog-autonomous-mowing-vs-traditional-ride-on-a-property-owner-s-guide.html).

*AutoAcre is an autonomous mowing operator based in the Northern Rivers, NSW, focused on solar-farm and commercial vegetation management. ben@autoacre.com.au*
meta: Robotic mower vs zero turn: a zero turn covers more per hour. The robot wins on hours it can run and frees skilled people. Honest limits both ways.

title: Is autonomous mowing actually cheaper than conventional mowing?
keyword: autonomous mowing vs conventional mowing cost
customBody:
**Is autonomous mowing actually cheaper than conventional mowing?**

Sometimes. It depends on how much planned work a site has and whether the machine has time to run, and the only honest way to find out is to measure it on the actual ground.

**Compare the job, not the day rate**

A machine day rate is the easy number to put side by side. It's also the wrong one.

Conventional mowing carries crew time, mobilisation, fuel, scheduling around site access, and the repeat visits a growing season forces. The bill for one visit is a single line. The cost of the cycle is the whole season, and [a week a month on the slasher](blog-a-week-a-month-on-the-slasher.html) is what that looks like on plenty of sites.

**Autonomous work has its own costs**

Setup and mapping. Transport between blocks. Technician time on site. Edges, posts and structures, which run 60 to 70 percent autonomous and get finished by people. Recovery when the machine stops, because it will.

Anyone quoting autonomous mowing without those lines in it is quoting a machine, not a job.

**What actually moves the numbers**

Two things. Enough planned work in one place, and enough time to run.

A machine planned at about 8 acres (3 hectares) a day does well on ground with weeks of repeating passes and permission to work outside daylight. The same machine on a small, cluttered, once-a-year block does not. We put the per-hour side of it together in [robot versus zero-turn: the real coverage maths](blog-robot-versus-zero-turn-the-real-coverage-maths.html).

Dense summer grass over 300 mm roughly halves speed, for machines and for crews. Whatever cycle you're costing, cost it wet as well as dry.

The work changes shape. Machines take the open repeatable passes. People do edges, structures, setup and the calls that need judgement. The role the machine creates is a skilled local technician, and that's a job with more in it, not less.

**The trial is the measurement**

We don't ask anyone to take the comparison on faith. Our model is to run a paid trial on the ground in question, log what the machine does on your grass and your slopes, and set that against the cycle you're running now.

You already know what your current cycle costs you. After a trial you'd know what ours does.

**Common questions**

### Is autonomous mowing always cheaper?

No. It can improve the economics where there's enough planned work and enough running time. On small or one-off sites it often doesn't.

### What gets left out of most comparisons?

Mobilisation, scheduling and repeat visits on the conventional side. Setup, transport, technician time and edge work on the autonomous side.

### How much ground does one machine cover?

We plan on about 8 acres (3 hectares) a day per machine, roughly halved in dense summer growth over 300 mm.

### Does this replace our mowing contractor?

No. It changes what the hours get spent on. Edges, posts and structures still need people.

### How long before we'd know?

Long enough to see a full cycle on the site, including one wet stretch. A single dry week tells you very little.

**Read next**

Related: [The biggest line item nobody budgets](blog-the-biggest-line-item-nobody-budgets.html), [Why autonomous mowing trials fail](blog-why-autonomous-mowing-trials-fail.html) and [The maths of a mowing cycle](blog-the-maths-of-a-mowing-cycle.html).

*AutoAcre is an autonomous mowing operator based in the Northern Rivers, NSW, focused on solar-farm and commercial vegetation management. ben@autoacre.com.au*
meta: Autonomous mowing vs conventional mowing cost: not automatically cheaper. It turns on planned work and running time. A paid trial is how you measure it.
